strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: proactive interference in long-context LLMs is a real, documented issue, and the paper nicely distinguishes 'internal working memory management' from the more commonly studied 'external memory' paradigm, offering a conceptually interesting complementary angle.

The Sculptor tool suite (fragmentation, summarize/fold/restore, search) is reasonably comprehensive and intuitively mapped onto human-like cognitive memory management strategies, which gives the framework a clear narrative and potential for follow-up work.

Reports consistent gains on NeedleBench Multi-Needle Reasoning across all three tested models (Claude-4-Sonnet, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3), with a sizable improvement for Claude-4-Sonnet (67.0 to 94.0 overall), and the gap widens with more needles/longer context, which is a coherent and intuitively explainable trend.

The illustrative example (Figure 1) and tool taxonomy communicate the idea clearly and the zero-shot nature of the approach (no fine-tuning required) is a practically appealing property if it held robustly.
weaknesses: Results are explicitly described as 'preliminary,' and the paper's core proposed training approach (multi-turn RL) is unfinished ('work in progress,' 'results are not yet available')—a central contribution claimed in the introduction is not actually delivered or evaluated.

Mixed and inconsistent results undermine the main claim: on PI-LLM, DeepSeek-V3 gets substantially worse with ACM tools (-5.93 points overall, and a drop from 100.00 to 53.48 at update count 2), and even Claude-4-Sonnet degrades sharply at low update counts (99.87→79.57), indicating the tools can actively hurt performance in some regimes rather than reliably help—this is not sufficiently analyzed or resolved.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual tools (fragmentation vs. fold/summary vs. search) to the observed gains, despite the paper claiming different tools dominate on different benchmarks; this claim is asserted rather than empirically substantiated.

No quantification of computational overhead: the paper explicitly acknowledges that ACM invalidates KV caching and increases computational cost, but provides no latency, token-cost, or wall-clock measurements, leaving the practical cost-benefit trade-off entirely unaddressed.

No variance/error bars reported despite repeating trials (5x for PI-LLM, 10x for NeedleBench), making it impossible to assess whether reported gains (or losses, e.g., for DeepSeek) are statistically meaningful or noise.

Very limited evaluation scope: only two benchmarks and three proprietary/closed models, no comparison to relevant external memory baselines discussed in related work (e.g., Mem0, MemOS, MemAgent), which would help contextualize whether ACM tools offer advantages over established alternatives.

Limited technical novelty: the individual tools (summarization, folding/hiding context, semantic search over context) are largely straightforward applications of existing context-compression and retrieval techniques repackaged as callable tools, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the contribution is primarily an engineering/prompting framework rather than a new method.

The paper is short and the methodology section is mostly descriptive tool listing without deeper analysis of tool-selection policies, failure modes, or interaction effects between tools, weakening the depth of the study for a top-tier venue.

Improvements on NeedleBench largely stem from search_context effectively performing standard retrieval-augmented reordering (appending relevant content at the end to combat lost-in-the-middle), which is a known mitigation strategy rather than a novel contribution of 'active context management' per se.

strengths: Proposes a conceptually interesting and complementary direction to external memory systems: enabling LLMs to actively curate their own working memory (fragment/fold/summarize/restore/search) rather than just retrieving from external stores.

The RL methodology (conditional trajectory collection + incremental loss assignment) meaningfully addresses a real technical challenge—non-monotonic context evolution when tools can remove/transform prior context—which breaks standard prefix-trajectory RL assumptions.

Fairly comprehensive empirical suite: zero-shot evaluation across three frontier models and two benchmarks, full RL training pipeline evaluated on five benchmarks, plus supporting analyses (attention allocation, context-length/cost reduction).
The attention analysis (Section 4.3) offers a plausible mechanistic explanation (reduced attention dilution) for why folding helps, going beyond pure end-task accuracy.
Tool design principles (determinism, reversibility, structural preservation) are well-motivated and the full JSON schemas are provided, aiding reproducibility of the tool interface itself.
Cost/context-length reduction analysis (Figure 6) is a useful practical contribution showing efficiency gains, not just accuracy gains.
weaknesses: The zero-shot results critically depend on hand-crafted, benchmark-specific system prompts (Section 4.1, Figures 7-8) that explicitly prescribe tool-call strategies (e.g., telling the model to fragment into exactly ten pieces and fold all but the last two-three). This undermines the paper's core narrative of LLMs exercising 'cognitive agency' — the improvements largely reflect prompt engineering, not autonomous active context management, and the 'unified prompt' unguided results show the tools often fail or backfire without this scaffolding.

Results are inconsistent across models: DeepSeek-V3 shows a net negative change on PI-LLM (-0.12) and mixed per-condition results even with task-specific prompts, undercutting claims of general effectiveness of ACM tools across model families.

The core RL model 'M3' is an undisclosed, proprietary 13B model 'pre-trained from scratch' with no architectural details, training corpus information, or public release, making the central RL results (Table 2, the paper's strongest quantitative claims) essentially unreproducible/unverifiable by external readers.

Gains on more holistic, less synthetic benchmarks (LongBenchV2: +1.5, FRAMES: -0.6) are marginal or negative, suggesting the method's benefits may be largely confined to synthetic/needle-style tasks with clear obsolete-information structure (PI-LLM, NeedleBench, MRCR) rather than generalizing to realistic long-context reasoning.

Training data for SFT/RL is generated by prompting Claude-4-Sonnet with the same hand-engineered task-specific prompts used in the zero-shot evaluation; this creates a degree of circularity and distillation-from-a-scaffolded-teacher rather than the model discovering strategies autonomously, weakening the 'self-sculpting' framing.

No comparison against strong existing context-compression baselines (e.g., LLMLingua/LongLLMLingua, StreamingLLM, SnapKV) is included in the main quantitative results, only discussed qualitatively in related work—leaving open whether simpler compression pipelines could match Sculptor's gains at lower complexity.

Table 2 and Table 1 report single-run point estimates with no variance/error bars or multiple seeds, and statistical significance is only checked for the narrow attention-analysis experiment (46 KV pairs from one benchmark), limiting confidence in the robustness of the main results.

The reward function is a simple sparse correctness/format signal; there is limited ablation isolating the contribution of the proposed incremental loss/conditional trajectory mechanism versus a naive alternative (e.g., training only on final trajectories), so the necessity of this specific RL innovation is asserted more than empirically isolated.

strengths: The paper introduces a coherent and well-engineered tool suite (fragment/fold/summarize/restore/search) for active context management, with clear JSON schemas provided for reproducibility of the tool interface itself.

The 'conditional trajectory collection with incremental loss assignment' addresses a real technical challenge in RL training when tool calls make context non-monotonic (ct not a subset of ct+1), which is a legitimate and somewhat novel contribution to multi-step agent RL training.

The value-specific attention analysis (Section 4.3) offers an interesting mechanistic angle, attempting to directly measure whether folding improves attention allocation to critical tokens rather than relying purely on downstream accuracy.
The cost analysis (context length reduction of ~76-89%) is a useful practical contribution if the accuracy gains hold up.
The related work section is reasonably thorough in situating the work relative to external memory, tool-use, and context-compression literature.
weaknesses: The core RL model 'M3' is an opaque, in-house 13B model 'pre-trained from scratch' with no architectural details disclosed, and Table 3 shows it substantially underperforms comparably-sized/larger open models on most standard benchmarks (e.g., LiveCodeBench 25.1 vs Kimi-K2 53.7, AIME 17.7 vs 69.6, MMLU-Pro 65.2 vs 81+). This raises serious concerns about reproducibility and about whether the large RL gains in Table 2 partly reflect fixing a weak/idiosyncratic baseline model rather than validating the general ACM concept.

The RAG and MemAgent baselines are deliberately weakened (BM25-only, no embeddings, ad hoc pseudo-queries when no query is given), which likely understates the true competitiveness of standard memory/retrieval approaches and inflates the apparent advantage of Sculptor.

Results are inconsistent across models and benchmarks: DeepSeek-V3 shows a net negative change on PI-LLM (-0.12) even after prompt optimization, and gains on the more realistic, less synthetic benchmarks (LongBenchV2: +1.5, FRAMES: -0.6) are marginal to negative — undermining the paper's central claims about broad applicability, which are further acknowledged in the Limitations section as 'modest.'

The main quantitative gains are concentrated on narrow, synthetic, needle/interference-style benchmarks (PI-LLM, NeedleBench-M-RS, MRCR) that are somewhat artificial constructs designed to showcase exactly the phenomena the tools are built to address, raising concerns about ecological validity and whether findings generalize to realistic long-context tasks.

The zero-shot (prompt-guided) results depend heavily on hand-crafted, benchmark-specific system prompts (Figs. 7-8) developed through iterative trial and error by the authors; this manual prompt engineering effort is substantial and not well disentangled from the intrinsic value of the tools themselves, weakening claims about 'leveraging LLMs' inherent tool-calling capabilities.'

No ablation isolating the contribution of individual tool categories (fragmentation vs. fold/summarize vs. search) to overall performance, making it hard to assess which components are actually driving the reported gains.

The search_context tool is limited to exact keyword matching (explicitly likened to Ctrl+F), which is a substantial limitation for real-world long-context tasks where relevant information is not expressible via exact string matches, yet the paper markets it under the broader 'search and retrieve' framing.
GSPO training hyperparameters (clip ratios of 0.0003/0.0004) appear unusually tight and are not justified or ablated, raising questions about the robustness/sensitivity of the training recipe.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting for most main results tables (Table 1, Table 2), aside from NeedleBench's 10 runs, making it difficult to assess whether reported deltas are robust.

The framing around 'cognitive agency,' 'sculpting,' and analogies to human cognitive psychology is largely rhetorical/narrative rather than rigorously grounded, and risks overclaiming the significance of what is fundamentally a tool-use + RL engineering contribution.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually distinct and interesting paradigm (Active Context Management) that complements external memory/RAG approaches by giving the LLM itself tools to fragment, fold, summarize, restore, and search its own conversation history—an intuitive analogy to human working-memory management.

The RL training methodology (conditional trajectory collection + incremental loss assignment) is a genuine technical contribution that addresses a real problem: standard multi-step RL assumes trajectory prefixes are preserved, but context-modifying tools break this assumption, and the proposed solution to avoid training collapse/redundant gradient signal is well-motivated and clearly described.

Broad empirical evaluation spanning five benchmarks (PI-LLM, NeedleBench-M-RS, MRCR, LongBenchV2, FRAMES) and multiple frontier models (Claude-4-Sonnet, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3) in the zero-shot setting, plus a dedicated RL-trained model comparison against RAG and MemAgent baselines.

The value-specific attention analysis and cost/context-length reduction analysis add useful mechanistic and practical insight beyond aggregate accuracy numbers, strengthening the paper's causal story about why folding helps.
Tool design principles (determinism, reversibility, structural preservation) are thoughtfully justified and directly support the tractability of the RL formulation.

Reasonably transparent reporting of failure modes (e.g., unguided tool-use inefficiencies, DeepSeek-V3 regression on PI-LLM, modest/negative results on LongBenchV2 and FRAMES), which lends some credibility to the claims.
weaknesses: The strong zero-shot gains substantially depend on hand-crafted, benchmark-specific system prompts (Fig. 7, 8) that essentially hard-code the optimal tool-use strategy for each benchmark (e.g., explicitly telling the model to fragment-then-fold for PI-LLM). This raises concerns that the demonstrated improvements partly reflect prompt engineering tailored to known benchmark structure rather than a generalizable emergent capability, and it is unclear how such prompts would be constructed for novel/unseen tasks.

The main RL results (Table 2) rely on a custom, non-public 13B base model (M3) whose baseline performance on standard reasoning/coding benchmarks (e.g., 17.7% AIME, 25.1% LiveCodeBench) is notably weaker than comparably sized or larger public models, raising reproducibility concerns and questions about whether the ACM/RL gains would transfer to stronger, more standard open or closed models.

Gains are inconsistent and sometimes negative on benchmarks requiring more holistic reasoning (LongBenchV2: +1.5, FRAMES: -0.6), suggesting the approach is primarily effective on synthetic, interference-heavy needle-style tasks rather than general long-context understanding—yet the abstract/framing implies broader robustness benefits.

Baselines for comparison (BM25-only RAG with a simple heuristic pseudo-query and fixed 1500-token budget; a single MemAgent configuration) may be relatively weak implementations, potentially inflating the apparent advantage of Sculptor; no comparison to other context-compression methods discussed in related work (e.g., LLMLingua) is included in the main quantitative table.

No ablation isolating the individual contribution of the incremental loss assignment / conditional trajectory collection versus a naive final-trajectory-only RL baseline, making it hard to verify how much of the Sculptor-M3-RL gain over Sculptor-M3 is attributable specifically to this proposed training innovation versus RL in general.

Limited statistical rigor in the main results tables (no variance/error bars reported for Table 1, 2 despite likely stochasticity in tool-calling trajectories), and DeepSeek-V3's negative net change on PI-LLM despite prompt optimization is not deeply analyzed.

The RL training data comes from only two source datasets (BABILong, GSM-Infinite), and while cross-benchmark transfer is shown, the diversity of tool-use scenarios covered during training may be limited relative to the diversity of evaluation benchmarks, which could affect the robustness of conclusions about generalization.
